summary.note: This edition replaces the previous one, which audited PRs #376-#389 against upstream v1.102.4; these ten rows are the ports merged after it, re-read diff by diff against the same revision, v1.102.4. Counted from the rows below and consistent with them: every `gaps` row has at least one entry in `findings`, every `faithful` row has none. summary.gate: Recorded in the top-level `gate` block. Green, after two environment adjustments named there.

gate.detail: All four steps green: `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test --all-targets` (37 test targets, 0 failed), `cargo build --release --bins`. Run at b41721d with CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=4, RUST_TEST_THREADS=4 and TS_RS_EXPERIMENT=this_is_unstable_software. Two environment facts were needed to get there, both about the machine and neither about the tree. First, it has to be run with an explicit `+1.95.0`: the default toolchain is a nightly with no clippy component installed, so `cargo clippy` there exits immediately with `'cargo-clippy' is not installed for the toolchain 'nightly-aarch64-apple-darwin'` without compiling anything. Second, the first run was red. `cargo test --all-targets` failed one test, tailnetd's `cleanup_refuses_live_socket`, with `path must be shorter than SUN_LEN`; the test binds a Unix socket under the temp directory, and the temp directory on this machine is 66 characters, which pushes the socket path past the 104-byte macOS limit. Re-running the whole gate with a short temp directory turns it green with no other change, and the same test passes on its own there, so the failure is the path length and not the code. The tests/parity_audit_ledger.rs contract over this file passed 6 of 6 against this edition.

auditedPrs.notes: The guard logic is a correct port. Upstream's `Start` consults the policy AuthKey only when an explicit key is absent, the node is not Running and no config file is in use, then skips it when profiles already exist unless the state is NeedsLogin; the fork reproduces all four conditions and the TrimSpace, and it is right that policy ranks LAST here. Two divergences. The diff's own quotation of upstream is of a `Start` that does not exist at the pinned ref, and the log text the port advertises as Go's follows the misquote rather than the real `by syspolicy` line. And the skip guard keys on whether the node has logged in, where upstream keys on pm.Profiles being non-empty, which are not the same predicate for a profile that exists but never completed a login.

Test-and-data only; it claims no upstream port and makes no behavioural claim about Go, so there is no upstream behaviour for it to diverge from. What it does claim is that the ledger contract was unsatisfiable once the audit moved past one edition's pull request numbers, and that holds: the replaced test hard-coded a specific PR's marker set. The replacement contract is internally consistent and is what this edition was written against — totals recomputed from the rows, a `gaps` row required to carry a finding, a `faithful` row required to carry none, and every upstream citation required to name a Go file at one pinned commit.

The central claim checks out exactly. Upstream's `runIP` refuses an empty address list before its match loop with `no current Tailscale IPs; state: %v`, it does so after the peer and Service resolution so an addressless peer is covered too, and it checks the empty list ahead of the per-family messages, so `-6` on an addressless node gets the empty-list sentence and not `no Tailscale IPv6 address`. All three are now reproduced, and the bare-stderr printing matches upstream's `main`. But the same diff leaves two error paths of the same two functions unported, and its own body lists them as not fixed. A stopped node still answers the daemon's `node is not up` where upstream prints the state-carrying sentence, which is the one case the pull request title names. And the `--assert` refusal is the fork's own sentence rather than upstream's `assertion failed` form, which also drops the address list upstream prints.

The nil-versus-empty port is exact. Upstream guards the whole advertised-routes block with a non-nil test, and JSON `[]` decodes to a non-nil empty slice, so an explicit empty list really does set the routes empty with the Set flag on and withdraw them; the fork's `Option<Vec<String>>` now carries that distinction and an absent key falls back to the persisted prefs. Both wording fixes hold too: upstream joins the bare route errors and its two callers wrap that join once as `error parsing config to prefs`, which the fork now does once rather than per offending route, and upstream formats the parsed prefix so the reported text is the normalised spelling. Test fixtures use the RFC 5737 and RFC 3849 documentation ranges. The set-level pairing rules applied in the same block are not in upstream's config loader, which checks only the masking rule; the diff discloses that in the code it adds and gives a deployment reason for it, so it is recorded here as a stated deviation rather than filed.

Upstream's `runWeb` really does run this step before the CGI branch and before it builds the server: it reads the status for the self address and the prefs for the web-client bit, and unless `--readonly` is set or the bit is already on it logs `starting tailscaled web client at http://<addr>` and turns the pref on, returning `starting web client in tailscaled: %w` if that fails. A failed prefs read leaves the bit false, so a node with no daemon logs the line and then fails, which is what the fork now does. The strings match verbatim, including `invalid AddrPort` for a node with no address, and the address is the first entry of the self address list as upstream takes it. The interrupt path matches too: upstream gates `stopping tailscaled web client` on not being in CGI mode and on this run having been the one that turned the bit on, logs a failure to turn it back off rather than returning it, and exits zero. Pinning the old CGI behaviour as parity was the error, and the test helper now passes `--readonly`, which is the invocation upstream answers that way.

The framing fix is right. Upstream singles this one refusal out, printing the cause itself followed by a blank separator and returning the help pointer, whose whole text is the try-help sentence, and `main` prints that bare; three lines of stderr, which is what the fork now produces. Moving this build's own `--service` gap behind upstream's checks is right too, and adding the mount-point cleaning ahead of the listener resolution matches upstream, wrapper text included. The order the diff reconstructs is not upstream's, though. It states that upstream runs both `--service` refusals and only then verifyFunnelEnabled, where upstream runs the funnel capability check between them, and the ported sequence has no funnel capability check at any point.

All three reported divergences check out against upstream and all three are removed. Upstream builds the refusal from a path error whose text is the C library string in Go's lowercased spelling with no errno number appended, so dropping Rust's trailing os-error suffix is the right shape. Upstream's directory creation returns the error of the one mkdir that failed, which names the topmost component it could not create rather than the whole requested path, and the fork now names that component. And upstream does return a stat failure on a parent directory bare, without the cannot-write-kubeconfig wrapper, which the fork now matches; the surrounding walk, the writability probe by temp-file create and remove for a directory and by a write-only open without create or truncate for a file, the wrapper wording and the mode on the final write all agree with upstream as well. Upstream's sandboxed-macOS arm of that wrapper stays omitted with a stated platform reason, which is a legitimate gate and is recorded rather than filed.

No code change, and the verification it records is accurate. Upstream's allowed-suggestions fill asks the policy client for a string array, returns a nil set when the key is absent, and builds a set from the decoded entries otherwise, so an unset key means no restriction and a configured empty list means nothing is permitted; the fork resolves the key to an optional set with exactly that nil-versus-empty rule and reads the decoded list rather than reparsing a rendered report row, so an identifier containing a space stays one identifier. The error path matches as well and is the half most worth getting right: upstream's caller logs the lookup error and leaves the set nil, which is no restriction, so recording an undecodable list as empty would stop every node with a malformed policy file from ever being suggested an exit node. Withholding an excluded suggestion yields the same empty result upstream returns when no candidate passes, not a new error shape.

Documentation only, and the precedence claim it corrects is the one upstream implements. Upstream's `Start` takes an explicitly supplied key first, then the config file's own key including its file-path indirection, and only then asks the policy client, and it asks only when no config file is in use at all. So for this one key policy really is consulted last, which is the opposite of how policy ranks for prefs, and the design document saying policy outranks the config file was contradicting both the code and upstream. Pinning the key's definition type in the guard test and pinning the never-enrolled-host case are the right things to hold: the whole failure this port removed was a key that is configured, reported and inert.

No code change, and the verification it records holds against upstream clause for clause. Upstream's up-args conversion splits the flag value on commas and, for any element containing no colon at all, prepends the tag prefix before validating; the condition really is a colon test and not a prefix test, so a value like `foo:bar` reaches the tag checker and is refused by name instead of quietly becoming a doubly-prefixed tag nobody asked for. The tag checker itself matches: cut the prefix, refuse an empty name, refuse a first byte that is not an ASCII letter, refuse any byte that is not a letter, a digit or a hyphen. The refusal quotes the completed value, which is upstream's format, and upstream's own flag help documents the prefix as optional. The report that prompted the branch is stale.

findings.title: The ported serve refusal order omits verifyFunnelEnabled, which upstream runs between the two --service refusals
findings.detail: The diff's body states upstream's order as: the two `--service` refusals, `verifyFunnelEnabled`, `cleanURLPath`, then `srvTypeAndPortFromFlags`, and `check_serve_flags` is built to that description. Upstream's `runServeCombined` does not run the two `--service` refusals together. It refuses `--service` with funnel, then runs `verifyFunnelEnabled(ctx, 443)` for the funnel subcommand, then refuses `--service` outside background mode, then cleans the mount point, then resolves the type and port. The funnel capability check is therefore ahead of the mount-point cleaning and ahead of the port refusal, and it is a daemon round trip that can refuse the command on its own. `verifyFunnelEnabled` has no counterpart anywhere in this repository's sources, so the step is not merely misordered but absent. Failure: on a node whose tailnet has not enabled funnel, `tnet funnel --set-path=/a/../b --https=70000` is refused with the mount-point wrapper, and after that is fixed with the too-high-port sentence, where upstream refuses both command lines first with the funnel capability error and never reaches either. The operator fixes two things that were never what stopped them.

findings.title: A stopped node still reports the daemon's "node is not up" instead of upstream's state-carrying sentence
findings.detail: The pull request's subject is that `tnet ip` should fail on an addressless target the way upstream does, and upstream's rule is one sentence for every addressless case: `no current Tailscale IPs; state: %v`, with the backend state read from the same status call. The merged change routes the self path through that sentence only when the daemon answers the `ip` request with an empty address pair. A stopped node does not; it answers with an error, and the fork prints `error: node is not up` and exits, so the one sentence the change exists to produce is not produced for the state that most often produces it. Upstream has no equivalent branch at all: `runIP` reads the status, finds an empty address list and reports `state: Stopped`. The diff's body lists this under work not fixed here, so it is disclosed, but it is a divergence from the behaviour of the very function the diff claims to port and it is reachable by the command in the subject line. Failure: `tnet ip` on a node brought down with `tnet down` prints `error: node is not up`; `tailscale ip` prints `no current Tailscale IPs; state: Stopped`. A script matching upstream's text, which is what the rest of this change exists to let it do, does not match.

findings.title: The policy auth-key log lines follow a misquoted upstream; the real Start logs "by syspolicy" with the key length
findings.detail: The merged code and its module documentation both quote upstream's `Start` as logging `Start: setting opts.AuthKey from syspolicy` and `Start: not setting opts.AuthKey from syspolicy; login profiles exist, state=%v`, inside an `if sysak != ""` with a nested profiles test. No such code is at the pinned ref. Upstream's block is flattened the other way: the skip case is the leading arm, its text is `not setting opts.AuthKey from syspolicy; login profiles exist, state=%v` with no `Start: ` prefix, and the take case logs `setting opts.AuthKey by syspolicy, len=%v` - `by syspolicy`, not `from syspolicy`, and carrying the key length, which is the only thing upstream reveals about the credential. The comments in `policy_auth_key` say the lines are logged the way upstream logs them and they are not, and the emitted text is a third wording again. Failure: an administrator debugging an MDM enrolment greps the daemon log for upstream's `setting opts.AuthKey by syspolicy` and finds nothing, on a node that took the policy key and enrolled with it; the length field that would tell them whether the key survived the plist round trip is not logged at all.

findings.title: The --assert refusal replaces upstream's "assertion failed" text and matches by parsed address rather than by string
findings.detail: Upstream's `--assert` compares the flag value against each of the node's addresses with a plain string comparison and, on no match, returns `assertion failed: IP %q not found among %v` - the value quoted as typed, followed by the list of addresses the node actually holds. The merged code parses the flag value first, refuses it as not a valid IP address if it does not parse, and on no match prints its own sentence naming only the parsed value and none of the node's addresses. Two behaviours move. Upstream never refuses an unparseable assertion; it simply fails the assertion, so `tailscale ip --assert=nonsense` exits 1 with the assertion-failed text, while the fork exits with a parse error of its own invention. And because the fork compares parsed addresses, a non-canonical spelling that upstream reports as a failed assertion is reported here as a success. The diff's body lists the text difference under work not fixed here; the parse refusal and the comparison change are not listed. Failure: `tnet ip --assert=100.064.000.001` exits 0 against a node holding 100.64.0.1; `tailscale ip --assert=100.064.000.001` exits 1, because the strings differ.

findings.title: The policy auth-key skip guard keys on having logged in, where upstream keys on pm.Profiles being non-empty
findings.detail: Upstream skips the policy auth key when `len(b.pm.Profiles()) > 0 && b.state != ipn.NeedsLogin` - the test is whether any login profile exists in the profile manager, not whether one of them ever completed a login. The merged gate supplies that input as the persisted prefs' logged-in flag. The two predicates differ for a profile that exists but has never enrolled, which is the state a node reaches after a profile is created and the login is abandoned or fails. Upstream treats that node as having profiles and declines the policy key unless the state is NeedsLogin; the fork treats it as not enrolled and uses the key. The direction matters: the guard exists so that dropping a policy file onto a host that already has profiles cannot silently re-register it, and widening the set of nodes that accept the key is the failure the guard is there to prevent. Failure: a host with an abandoned half-created profile and a policy file carrying an AuthKey enrols itself from that key on the next start; upstream logs `not setting opts.AuthKey from syspolicy; login profiles exist` and leaves it alone.
